newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Nomura chief has vital overseas experience.
newsitem.headline: New Nomura chief has vital overseas experience.

text.p: Nomura Securities' next president, Junichi Ujiie, has the overseas experience analysts say is vital as the scandal-tainted Japanese brokerage strives to regain credibility and cope with a deregulated market.

Nomura said on Tuesday that Ujiie, now a managing director, will take over on May 1 as president in a sweeping management shake-up the brokerage hopes will repair its image, tainted by a scandal over illegal deals linked to a racketeer.

The management house-cleaning will remove Masashi Suzuki from his post as president, which he assumed just over one month ago when his predecessor stepped down over the scandal. Suzuki will remain as chairman, but without representative rights. In addition, 15 board members including five vice-presidents will resign their posts to become advisers.
"I must make the utmost effort to restore trust (in Nomura) as quickly as possible," Ujiie told a news conference.

Ujiie, 51, has a doctorate in economics from the University of Chicago and was appointed president of New York-based Nomura Securities International in 1989. He held the post of chairman of that unit, was in charge of Nomura's overall American operations between June 1992 and May 1996, and has been a managing director since 1995.

Prosecutors and Japan's securities watchdog are investigating Nomura for deals linked to a "sokaiya," a type of of racketeer who typically extorts money from firms by threatening to disrupt their shareholders' meetings.
On Tuesday, Suzuki's predecessor, Hideo Sakamaki, told a parliamentary panel that Nomura had paid more than 70 million yen ($555,000) via stock accounts linked to a racketeer.

A domestic media report, meanwhile, said that the Finance Ministry was likely to suspend some of Nomura's operations, including stock dealing on its own account, for about three months as a punishment for the scandal.

"If they had selected a vice president or an executive managing director to become president, he would have been caught up in old-style practices and ways of thinking, so it would have been tough to really reform Nomura's way of doing business," said one Japanese financial analyst.
"What Nomura needs most now is globalisation, so the choice (of Ujiie) is very fitting," he added.

Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSCB James Capel, said Ujiie would need to draw on his experience to help the brokerage repair the damage done to its reputation by the scandal -- its second in six years -- and meet the challenges posed by Japan's "Big Bang" financial deregulation programme.

"Hopefully, the move (the management changes) represents an attempt by Nomura to clean its house, to stem any further loss of credibility, to prevent further defections from its own client base, and to install someone with the broad domestic and international experience which will be essential as Nomura moves to position itself for the 'Big Bang'," Waterhouse said.

Japan has pledged to bring down barriers among brokerages, banks and insurers and to open up its financial markets in a "Big Bang" reform by the year 2001 in an effort to catch up with New York and London as a financial centre. ($1=126 yen)
